headline: High: LightAgent’s broad egress and MCP/browser tooling paired with Pipecat’s shared-bus, multi-service runtime creates default risks of leakage, prompt injection, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent can use MCP, browsers, and stdin/stdout, so it can ingest external content; Pipecat runs on a shared bus with multiple instances, so outputs can propagate across sessions. The pairwise bridge is plausible in default integrations, but no direct proof of a raw-instructions channel exists, so medium is the higher justified severity.
conditions: IF LightAgent forwards browser or MCP content into Pipecat without provenance filtering
IF Pipecat consumers treat shared-bus text as instructions
mitigations: Disable MCP ingestion for untrusted sources
Add provenance tags to all cross-agent messages
Strip executable markup before passing outputs between agents
Route only structured JSON between agents
requires-engineering: enforce allowlisted message schemas at the bus boundary

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent touches conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and secrets, while Pipecat handles text, conversation state, and can call many third-party STT/LLM/TTS services via allowlisted egress. That creates a default exfiltration path for sensitive content from A into B’s external APIs, with meaningful leakage risk and no built-in isolation shown.
conditions: IF LightAgent passes secrets or memory into Pipecat inputs
IF Pipecat is configured to use any external STT/LLM/TTS provider
mitigations: Remove secrets from cross-agent payloads
Use local-only Pipecat providers
Redact conversation memory before handoff
Turn off analytics/telemetry exports
requires-engineering: add DLP filters at the integration boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LightAgent supports multiple instances and subprocesses, and Pipecat explicitly shares state on a bus across instances. Even without filesystem overlap, both can mutate shared conversational state or workflow state, so write conflicts are plausible in default deployments. The exact shared resource is not specified, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same shared bus or workflow state
IF no external locking or transaction layer is present
mitigations: Assign one writer per shared resource
Serialize updates through a queue
Add optimistic concurrency checks
Separate per-agent state namespaces
requires-engineering: introduce distributed locking or transactional storage

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent can emit tool results, errors, and provenance metadata, and Pipecat’s shared-bus design makes it likely to consume upstream outputs as live session state. If Pipecat acts on those outputs without verification, a mistaken or malicious A output can cascade into downstream speech, routing, or API actions. The blast radius spans multiple work products and can be irreversible.
conditions: IF Pipecat treats LightAgent outputs as authoritative session state
IF downstream Pipecat services trigger external actions from that state
mitigations: Require human review for action-bearing outputs
Validate A outputs against schemas before use
Keep A outputs read-only until checked
Log and diff all state transitions
requires-engineering: add verification gates before any external action

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent explicitly handles secrets and long-term memory, while Pipecat documents broad third-party service integrations and analytics/metrics. Even without a named residency mismatch, the pair can move regulated or sensitive data into external processors and telemetry paths, creating a compliance gap in default integrations. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from the interaction, not either one alone.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in LightAgent memory or tool results
IF Pipecat routes that data to external STT/LLM/TTS or analytics services
mitigations: Classify data before handoff
Disable telemetry for regulated sessions
Use region-locked providers only
Document retention and deletion paths
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
